meta.titre: Simple Harmonic Motion of a Particle: From the equation to period, speed and timing
tags: simple harmonic motion of a particle

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Further Mathematics past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: When a minibus from Bafoussam drives over a speed bump, the body of the vehicle bounces up and down on its springs and gradually settles. A guitar string, a swing pushed gently in a village playground and the needle of a sewing machine all repeat their motion in the same regular way. In Further Mathematics the simplest such motion is modelled exactly and described by a short list of results that connect the period, the amplitude and the speed. Questions on this appear in almost every Paper 3, usually with an elastic string and a request for a time or a maximum speed.

items: Acceleration is $\ddot x=\dfrac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}}$ and velocity is $v=\dot x$, and the identity $\ddot x=v\dfrac{dv}{dx}$ holds.
The sine and cosine functions have period $2\pi$, and calculators must be set to radians when the argument is a time-dependent angle.
Hooke's law: the tension in an elastic string of natural length $l$ and modulus of elasticity $\lambda$ with extension $y$ is $T=\dfrac{\lambda y}{l}$.
Newton's second law: resultant force $=$ mass $\times$ acceleration.

sections.titre: Simple harmonic motion: the defining equation and its results
sections.contenu_markdown:
A particle moves in **simple harmonic motion** (SHM) about a point $O$ when its acceleration is always directed towards $O$ and is proportional to its displacement $x$ from $O$:

$$
\ddot x=-\omega^{2}x\tag{1}
$$

with $\omega>0$ constant (in $\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$). The general solution is $x=a\cos(\omega t+\varepsilon)$, and the useful special cases are $x=a\sin\omega t$ (the particle is at $O$ when $t=0$) and $x=a\cos\omega t$ (the particle is at an extreme position when $t=0$). Here $a>0$ is the **amplitude**.

Writing $\ddot x=v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=-\omega^{2}x$ and integrating, with $v=0$ when $x=\pm a$, gives the speed at any position:

$$
v^{2}=\omega^{2}\left(a^{2}-x^{2}\right)\tag{2}
$$

The main results are:

| Quantity | Value | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Period | $T=\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$ (frequency $\dfrac1T$) | |
| Maximum speed | $a\omega$ | at $O$, where $x=0$ |
| Maximum acceleration | $\omega^{2}a$ | at the ends, where $x=\pm a$ and $v=0$ |
| Acceleration at $O$ | $0$ | |

The period does not depend on the amplitude. To find the time between two positions, use $x=a\sin\omega t$ (or the cosine form) and solve for $t$ in radians.

variantes.nom: Vertical oscillations on an elastic string
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a particle hangs from an elastic string or spring and is displaced vertically.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Let the string have natural length $l$ and modulus $\lambda$, and carry a particle of mass $m$. At equilibrium the extension is $e=\dfrac{mgl}{\lambda}$. Let $x$ be the displacement **downwards from the equilibrium position**. Then
$$
m\ddot x=mg-\frac{\lambda(e+x)}{l}=-\frac{\lambda}{l}\,x\tag{3}
$$
so the motion is SHM with $\omega^{2}=\dfrac{\lambda}{ml}$. This holds only while the string is taut, that is while $a\le e$. The tension at displacement $x$ is $\dfrac{\lambda(e+x)}{l}$. A spring, which can also be compressed, behaves the same way for all displacements.

variantes.nom: Finding $\omega$ and $a$ from two data points
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the speeds at two distances from $O$ are given.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Apply (2) twice: $v_{1}^{2}=\omega^{2}(a^{2}-x_{1}^{2})$ and $v_{2}^{2}=\omega^{2}(a^{2}-x_{2}^{2})$. Subtracting eliminates $a^{2}$ and gives $\omega^{2}=\dfrac{v_{1}^{2}-v_{2}^{2}}{x_{2}^{2}-x_{1}^{2}}$. Then substitute back to find $a$.

variantes.nom: Time to travel between two positions
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked for the time taken to go from one position to another.
variantes.contenu_markdown: With $x=a\sin\omega t$ the particle is at $x$ when $t=\dfrac1\omega\arcsin\dfrac xa$. For two positions $x_{1}<x_{2}$ reached in the same direction on the same side of $O$ the time between them is $\dfrac{1}{\omega}\left(\arcsin\dfrac{x_{2}}{a}-\arcsin\dfrac{x_{1}}{a}\right)$. Use radians.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A particle $P$ moves along a straight line. Its acceleration is always directed towards a fixed point $O$ of the line and has magnitude $16x\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, where $x$ metres is the distance $OP$. When $P$ is $0.3\ \mathrm{m}$ from $O$ its speed is $1.6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Find

(a) the amplitude and the period of the motion,

(b) the maximum speed and the maximum acceleration of $P$,

(c) the time taken by $P$ to travel directly from $O$ to the point $0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ from $O$.

etapes.justification: The acceleration is towards $O$ and proportional to $x$, so $\ddot x=-\omega^{2}x$ with $\omega^{2}=16$.
Use $v^{2}=\omega^{2}(a^{2}-x^{2})$ with the given speed and position.

etapes.action: Find the maximum speed and acceleration.
etapes.justification: Maximum speed at $O$ is $a\omega$; maximum acceleration at the ends is $\omega^{2}a$.
Take $t=0$ at $O$, so $x=a\sin\omega t$; work in radians.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The amplitude is $0.5\ \mathrm{m}$ and the period is $\dfrac\pi2\approx1.57\ \mathrm{s}$. The maximum speed is $2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and the maximum acceleration is $8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. The particle takes $\dfrac{\pi}{24}\approx0.131\ \mathrm{s}$ to go from $O$ to the point $0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ away.

items.erreur_markdown: A student solves $\sin4t=\dfrac12$ with the calculator in degree mode and gets $4t=30$.
items.pourquoi_faux: In $x=a\sin\omega t$ the argument $\omega t$ is in radians, because $\omega$ is in $\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. Degree mode gives a wrong time.

items.erreur_markdown: A student writes the speed formula as $v^{2}=\omega^{2}\left(a^{2}+x^{2}\right)$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The speed must be zero at the ends $x=\pm a$ and largest at the centre. With a plus sign it would never be zero and would grow with $|x|$.

items.erreur_markdown: A student takes the period as $T=\dfrac{\omega}{2\pi}$ and for $\omega=4$ gets $T=0.64\ \mathrm{s}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The quantity $\dfrac{\omega}{2\pi}$ is the frequency (oscillations per second), not the period. A larger $\omega$ means a faster motion and so a shorter period.

items.erreur_markdown: A particle hangs on an elastic string. A student measures $x$ from the natural length and writes $m\ddot x=-\dfrac{\lambda x}{l}$ as the equation of motion.
items.pourquoi_faux: Measured from the natural length, the weight also acts, so the equation is $m\ddot x=mg-\dfrac{\lambda x}{l}$, which is not of the form $-\omega^{2}x$. The motion is SHM about the equilibrium position, not about the natural length.
items.correction_markdown: Measure $x$ from the equilibrium position, where the extension is $e=mgl/\lambda$. Then $m\ddot x=-\dfrac{\lambda x}{l}$.

items.erreur_markdown: A student says the acceleration is greatest at the centre of the motion because the speed is greatest there.
items.pourquoi_faux: The acceleration is $-\omega^{2}x$, so it is zero at the centre and has its largest magnitude $\omega^{2}a$ at the ends, where the speed is zero.
items.correction_markdown: Maximum speed $a\omega$ at $x=0$; maximum acceleration $\omega^{2}a$ at $x=\pm a$.

items.enonce_markdown:
The displacement of a particle from a fixed point $O$ at time $t$ seconds is $x=0.2\cos5t$ metres.

(a) Write down the amplitude and find the period, correct to $3$ significant figures.

(b) Find the maximum speed and the maximum acceleration.

(c) Find the speed of the particle when $x=0.12\ \mathrm{m}$.
items.solution_markdown:
Comparing with $x=a\cos\omega t$: $a=0.2$ and $\omega=5$.

(a) Amplitude **$0.2\ \mathrm{m}$**. Period $T=\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\approx$ **$1.26\ \mathrm{s}$**.

(b) Maximum speed $a\omega=0.2\times5=$ **$1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$**. Maximum acceleration $\omega^{2}a=25\times0.2=$ **$5.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$**.

(c) $v^{2}=25\left(0.2^{2}-0.12^{2}\right)=25\times0.0256=0.64$, so $v=$ **$0.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$**.

items.enonce_markdown:
A particle of mass $0.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length $0.6\ \mathrm{m}$ and modulus of elasticity $30\ \mathrm{N}$. The other end is fixed to a point $A$ and the particle hangs in equilibrium vertically below $A$. Take $g=9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. The particle is pulled down a further $0.04\ \mathrm{m}$ and released from rest.

(a) Find the extension of the string in equilibrium.

(b) Show that the particle moves in SHM and find the period.

(c) Find the maximum speed of the particle and the greatest tension in the string.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $e=\dfrac{mgl}{\lambda}=\dfrac{0.5\times9.8\times0.6}{30}=$ **$0.098\ \mathrm{m}$**.

(b) Let $x$ be the displacement below the equilibrium position. Then $m\ddot x=mg-\dfrac{\lambda(e+x)}{l}$. Since $mg=\dfrac{\lambda e}{l}$, this gives $0.5\ddot x=-\dfrac{30}{0.6}x$, that is $\ddot x=-100x$. This is SHM with $\omega=10\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. The amplitude is $0.04\ \mathrm{m}$, which is less than $0.098\ \mathrm{m}$, so the string stays taut. Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{10}=\dfrac{\pi}{5}\approx$ **$0.628\ \mathrm{s}$**.

(c) Maximum speed $=a\omega=0.04\times10=$ **$0.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$**. The greatest tension is at the lowest point, where the extension is $0.098+0.04=0.138\ \mathrm{m}$: $\dfrac{30\times0.138}{0.6}=$ **$6.9\ \mathrm{N}$**.

items.enonce_markdown:
A particle moves in simple harmonic motion along a straight line with centre $O$. When it is $0.6\ \mathrm{m}$ from $O$ its speed is $4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and when it is $0.8\ \mathrm{m}$ from $O$ its speed is $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

(a) Find the angular frequency $\omega$ and the amplitude of the motion.

(b) Find the maximum acceleration.

(c) Find the time taken by the particle to travel directly from the point $0.6\ \mathrm{m}$ from $O$ to the point $0.8\ \mathrm{m}$ from $O$ on the same side of $O$, giving your answer in seconds correct to $3$ significant figures.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $16=\omega^{2}(a^{2}-0.36)$ and $9=\omega^{2}(a^{2}-0.64)$. Subtracting: $7=\omega^{2}(0.64-0.36)=0.28\,\omega^{2}$, so $\omega^{2}=25$ and **$\omega=5\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$**. Then $a^{2}=0.36+\dfrac{16}{25}=1$, so the amplitude is **$1\ \mathrm{m}$**.

(b) Maximum acceleration $=\omega^{2}a=25\times1=$ **$25\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$**.

(c) With $x=\sin5t$ (measuring time from $O$): $x=0.6$ at $t_{1}=\dfrac{\arcsin0.6}{5}\approx0.1287\ \mathrm{s}$ and $x=0.8$ at $t_{2}=\dfrac{\arcsin0.8}{5}\approx0.1855\ \mathrm{s}$. The time between them is $t_{2}-t_{1}\approx$ **$0.0568\ \mathrm{s}$**.

items_markdown: SHM means $\ddot x=-\omega^{2}x$; the amplitude is $a$ and the period is $T=\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$, independent of $a$.
Speed at displacement $x$: $v^{2}=\omega^{2}(a^{2}-x^{2})$. Maximum speed $a\omega$ at the centre; maximum acceleration $\omega^{2}a$ at the ends.
For an elastic string, measure $x$ from the equilibrium position, where the extension is $mgl/\lambda$; then $\omega^{2}=\dfrac{\lambda}{ml}$, valid while the string is taut.
Two speed-position pairs give $\omega^{2}$ by subtraction, then $a$ by substitution.
For times use $x=a\sin\omega t$ or $x=a\cos\omega t$ with the calculator in radians.
